contextQuestions.prompt: Other methodology/framework labels the organization uses

coreItems.prompt: Major requirements are expected to be substantially defined before implementation begins.
Release scope is committed well before the work needed to deliver it is complete.
Changes discovered after implementation begins normally require formal change approval.
Design, build, test, and release milestones are managed against an upfront baseline plan.
Delivery success is judged primarily by conformance to the original scope/schedule plan.
New customer or operational evidence can change upcoming priorities through the normal process.
The team can clarify or renegotiate planned scope when it learns something important.
Findings from implementation regularly change what the team plans to do next.
Stakeholder feedback can alter priorities without waiting for a major project phase boundary.
Planning is revisited often enough that newly learned information can materially affect near-term work.
Work is organized in consistent short iterations or timeboxes.
Each iteration has a shared outcome or goal rather than only a collection of assigned tasks.
Planning, inspection/review, and improvement happen on a consistent iteration cadence.
The team aims to produce usable, integrated work by the end of each iteration.
Work that has not met the team's completion/quality criteria is not counted as finished merely because the iteration ended.
The team has an explicit shared definition of how work moves from started to finished.
The amount of work in progress is explicitly controlled.
New work is normally started when capacity becomes available rather than simply when it is assigned.
The team uses flow evidence such as cycle time, throughput, work-item age, or equivalent measures.
Aging, blocked, or stalled work is actively reviewed and managed.
The stable delivery team collectively has most skills needed to turn an idea into usable software.
Product, development, and quality work happens collaboratively rather than as separate sequential departments.
People are generally kept with a stable team rather than reassigned among projects whenever demand changes.
The team remains responsible for work until it is usable/releasable rather than stopping at a specialist handoff.
Dependencies on people outside the team are exceptions rather than the normal path for completing ordinary work.
Work commonly waits in queues between analysis, development, QA, security, operations, or release functions.
One function completes an artifact or phase and formally hands it to another function to continue.
Development work is commonly considered complete before downstream testing begins.
A separate release or operations function must normally take ownership before software can be delivered.
Progress is commonly tracked by completion of functional phases such as requirements, development, testing, and release.
Completion/quality expectations are known before implementation is considered finished.
Developers routinely verify their own work rather than relying on QA to discover ordinary defects.
QA/test expertise participates early enough to influence examples, acceptance criteria, or design.
Automated tests and other quality checks run as part of the routine delivery pipeline.
Defects found during delivery are normally resolved within the same working flow rather than accumulated for a later test/fix phase.
Work commonly requires approval outside the delivery team before it can move to the next major stage.
Releases commonly require formal signoff, a release board, or a comparable external gate.
Material scope changes normally require approval from management/governance outside the team/product owner.
Formal phase or milestone gates determine when the team may proceed.
Functional signoffs are required before work is considered complete even when the delivery team believes it is usable.
Stakeholders regularly inspect working software or actual outcomes rather than relying primarily on status reports.
Retrospectives or equivalent improvement reviews result in observable changes to how the team works.
Delivery/product decisions use evidence from actual results rather than only forecasts and plan completion.
The team intentionally runs small experiments or incremental changes to reduce uncertainty.
When results differ from assumptions, plans or working methods are changed promptly.
The team decides how to perform the work needed to achieve its near-term goal.
Developers/team members participate directly in selecting and planning the work they can complete.
Day-to-day work is not primarily assigned person-by-person by a manager or coordinator.
The team can make ordinary technical and execution tradeoffs without seeking external approval.
Team members can reorganize their work when conditions change without waiting for a manager to rewrite the task plan.
Completed software can be released independently of a large scheduled batch when the organization chooses to do so.
Build/test/deployment automation supports moving changes toward production routinely.
The team integrates changes continuously enough to avoid long-lived stabilization periods.
A separate code-freeze/regression phase is not normally required to make a release safe.
Production/user feedback can reach the team soon enough to influence subsequent delivery decisions.
Teams are organized around persistent products/services/value streams more than temporary projects.
A clearly accountable product decision-maker can continuously reorder upcoming work.
Success is discussed in terms of customer/business outcomes in addition to scope and schedule delivery.
Discovery and delivery interact continuously rather than discovery ending before delivery begins.
Funding/planning/ownership supports continued product evolution after an individual project or release ends.

SDRA-SM.prompt: The Scrum Master/facilitator coaches the team to manage its own work.
The Scrum Master/facilitator helps the organization remove impediments the team cannot remove itself.
Retrospective learning is turned into concrete changes with help from the Scrum Master/facilitator.
The Scrum Master/facilitator helps stakeholders and the team improve collaboration rather than acting mainly as a status intermediary.
The Scrum Master/facilitator spends substantial effort scheduling ceremonies, collecting status, and maintaining process administration.
The Scrum Master/facilitator is held responsible for enforcing delivery dates or individual task completion.
The Scrum Master/facilitator assigns work or directs day-to-day execution.
The Scrum Master/facilitator simultaneously performs a project-manager or line-manager role for the same team's ordinary delivery work.

SDRA-QA.prompt: QA/test specialists participate before implementation is complete.
QA/test expertise helps shape acceptance criteria, examples, test strategy, or design.
Quality is treated as the responsibility of the whole delivery team.
Routine regression/verification is substantially automated and part of normal delivery.
Completed development normally waits for a QA phase or QA queue before it can progress.
QA approval outside the development team is normally required before release.
QA is expected to discover defects that developers could reasonably have detected before handoff.
Testing occurs primarily after the planned development work for a feature/release is complete.

SDRA-DEV.prompt: Developers help decide how much work the team can take on and how it will be implemented.
Developers collaborate directly with product and QA/test rather than communicating primarily through coordinators.
Developers remain responsible for work through verification and usable/releasable state.
Developers routinely participate in production/support learning for the software they build.
Developers are frequently reassigned among projects according to utilization or resource demand.
Developer work is considered complete when coding is finished and the item is handed to another function.
Daily tasks are commonly assigned to individual developers by someone outside the developer group.
Developers participate in discovery/refinement and can influence scope or solution choices before coding begins.

SDRA-PM.prompt: The project manager primarily coordinates dependencies, external commitments, budget, or governance without directing the team's daily execution.
The project manager helps remove cross-team/organizational constraints that the delivery team cannot resolve itself.
The project manager is the central owner of detailed scope, schedule, and delivery-plan conformance.
The project manager assigns or redistributes day-to-day work among team members.
Material changes to planned work normally require project-manager approval or escalation.
Team status primarily flows upward through the project manager rather than being visible from working results/flow.
The project manager performs responsibilities the organization also describes as Scrum Master responsibilities.
The project manager's role is mainly necessary because delivery crosses many organizational, vendor, governance, or contractual boundaries.

SDRA-PROD.prompt: A clearly accountable product decision-maker can reorder the backlog when evidence changes.
Stakeholders who want priority changes normally work through that accountable product decision-maker rather than assigning work directly to the team.
Product decisions are tied to customer/user/business outcomes rather than only project scope completion.
Product/stakeholder feedback is gathered frequently enough to alter upcoming work.
The product decision-maker is expected to obtain committee/management approval for ordinary backlog reprioritization.
The backlog mainly represents execution of a scope already committed in a project plan.
Discovery of customer/problem/solution evidence continues while delivery is underway.
The product role has authority over priority but does not assign developers' detailed execution tasks.

scoring.organizationAggregationDefault: Equal weight across privacy-eligible role cohorts after respondent-level scoring

similarity: 100 - weightedMean(abs(observedDimension - archetypeDimension)); equal weights in pilot

visualization.note: Axes are descriptive and are not uniformly 'higher is better'.

sourceBasis: Manifesto for Agile Software Development and Principles
